q: 101. The thermal or temperature stress is a function of
explain: Thermal stress is calculated using the formula σ = αtE, where α is the coefficient of linear expansion, t is the temperature change, and E is the Modulus of Elasticity.

q: 102. When a circular bar tapering uniformly from diameter d1 at one end to d2 at the other end, is subjected to an increase in temperature (t), then the thermal stress induced is
explain: For a tapering bar, the stress varies along the length. The maximum thermal stress developed when the ends are fixed is (α * t * E * d1) / d2.

q: 103. The deformation of the bar per unit length in the direction of the force is known as
explain: Linear strain (or longitudinal strain) is defined as the ratio of change in length to the original length in the direction of the applied force.

q: 104. Every direct stress is always accompanied by a strain in its own direction and an opposite kind of strain in every direction at right angles to it. Such a strain is known as
explain: Lateral strain occurs perpendicular to the direction of the applied load. If a bar is stretched, it shortens in its transverse dimensions.

q: 105. The ratio of the lateral strain to the linear strain is called
explain: Poisson's ratio (μ) is a constant for a material within the elastic limit, representing the ratio of lateral strain to longitudinal strain.

q: 106. The Poisson's ratio for steel varies from
explain: For most engineering metals like steel, Poisson's ratio typically falls between 0.25 and 0.33.

q: 107. The Poisson's ratio for cast iron varies from
explain: Cast iron is more brittle than steel and generally has a lower Poisson's ratio, typically ranging from 0.23 to 0.27.

q: 108. When a bar of length l, width b and thickness t is subjected to a pull of P, its
options: length increases, width and thickness decreases
length decreases, width and thickness increases
explain: Under a tensile pull, the material elongates in the direction of the force (length increases) and contracts in the transverse directions (width and thickness decrease).

q: 109. The ratio of change in volume to the original volume is called
explain: Volumetric strain (εv) is the change in volume (dV) divided by the original volume (V).

q: 110. When a bar of length l, width b and thickness t is subjected to a push of P, its
options: length increases, width and thickness decreases
length decreases, width and thickness increases
explain: Under a compressive push, the bar shortens (length decreases) and expands laterally (width and thickness increase).

q: 111. The volumetric strain is the ratio of the
options: original thickness to the change in thickness
change in thickness to the original thickness
original volume to the change in volume
change in volume to the original volume
explain: Volumetric strain measures the overall deformation of a body in terms of volume change relative to its initial state.

q: 112. When a body is subjected to three mutually perpendicular stresses, of equal intensity, the ratio of direct stress to the corresponding volumetric strain is
explain: Bulk Modulus (K) is the ratio of direct stress to volumetric strain when a body is subjected to equal stresses in all three directions.

q: 113. The ratio of bulk modulus to Young's modulus for a Poisson's ratio of 0.25 will be
explain: Using the relation E = 3K(1 - 2μ). If μ = 0.25, then E = 3K(1 - 0.5) = 1.5K. Therefore, K/E = 1/1.5 = 2/3.

q: 114. The ratio of shear modulus to the modulus of elasticity for a Poisson's ratio of 0.4 will be
explain: Using the relation E = 2G(1 + μ). If μ = 0.4, then E = 2G(1.4) = 2.8G. Therefore, G/E = 1/2.8 = 5/14.

q: 115. The Young's modulus of a material is 125 GPa and Poisson's ratio 0.25. The modulus of rigidity of the material is
116. Within elastic limit, shear stress is ___________ shear strain.
explain: According to Hooke's Law for shear, shear stress is directly proportional to shear strain within the elastic limit.

q: 117. Shear modulus is the ratio of
explain: Shear Modulus (or Modulus of Rigidity, G) is defined as the ratio of shear stress to shear strain.

q: 118. A localized compressive stress at the area of contact between two members is known as
explain: Crushing stress (or bearing stress) is the localized compressive stress at the surface of contact between two relative parts.

q: 119. In a bar of large length when held vertically, its own weight produces additional stress. The maximum stress will be
options: at every point of the bar
explain: The top cross-section must support the weight of the entire bar below it, making the stress maximum at the support.

q: 120. If the stress produced by a prismatic bar is equal to the working stress, the area of the cross-section becomes
explain: This refers to the theoretical 'limit of length' for a bar under its own weight; if the self-weight stress equals the allowed stress, any increase in length would require an infinite area to maintain that stress level.

q: 121. The ratio of elongations of a conical bar due to its own weight and that of a prismatic bar of the same length, is
explain: Elongation of prismatic bar = γL²/2E. Elongation of conical bar = γL²/6E. The ratio is (1/6) / (1/2) = 1/3.

q: 122. If all the dimensions of a bar are increased in the proportion n:1, the proportion of maximum stress will increase in the ratio
explain: Stress due to self-weight is σ = γL. If all dimensions increase by n, the new length is nL, so stress becomes n(γL), a ratio of n:1.

q: 123. If the stress in each cross-section of a pillar is equal to its working stress, it is called
explain: A body of equal strength is designed so that the stress is constant at all sections, usually by varying the cross-sectional area.

q: 124. A member with cross-section A mm² is subjected to a force P N. It is L mm long. The linear strain will be
explain: Stress σ = P/A. Strain ε = σ/E = P/(AE). Strain is dimensionless (mm/mm).

q: 125. Young's Modulus is the ratio of the normal stress to the
explain: By definition, Young's Modulus is the constant of proportionality between normal stress and normal strain within the limit of proportionality.

q: 126. As per elastic theory of design, the factor of safety is the ratio of
options: unlimited load to load at yield
explain: Factor of Safety (FOS) is defined as the ratio of the failure stress (yield stress for ductile materials) to the allowable or working stress.

q: 127. In a composite bar, the load distribution... is based on the assumption that all the materials will have
explain: For composite bars subjected to axial loads, the fundamental compatibility condition is that the change in length is the same for all components, meaning they undergo the same strain.

q: 128. The stress due to temperature change in a member depends on
options: supporting conditions at the two ends
explain: Thermal stress only develops if the expansion or contraction of the member is restricted by the supporting conditions (e.g., fixed ends).

q: 129. In a Uniaxial tension test on a mild steel bar, the Lueders' lines will be
options: inclined at 45° to the direction of tensile stress
perpendicular to the direction of tensile stress
along the direction of tensile stress
explain: Lueders' lines (or slip lines) appear due to shear failure, which occurs on planes of maximum shear stress, typically inclined at 45° to the axis of tensile loading.

q: 130. The percentage elongation of a material from a direct tensile test indicates
explain: Ductility is the property that allows a material to undergo significant plastic deformation before rupture, measured by percentage elongation.

q: 131. The percentage reduction in area of a member from a direct tension test indicates
explain: Like elongation, the reduction in cross-sectional area at the point of fracture is a key measure of a material's ductility.

q: 132. The Poisson's ratio is the ratio of
options: Yong's Modulus elasticity to Modulus of Rigidity
explain: Poisson's ratio is the ratio of transverse (lateral) strain to axial (longitudinal) strain.

q: 133. A tie is a member which
options: is subjected to axial tension primarily
explain: In structural engineering, a 'tie' is a tension member designed to resist forces that pull it apart.

q: 134. A strut is member which
options: is subjected to shear force predominantly
is subjected to axial compressive predominantly
explain: A strut is a structural component designed to resist longitudinal compression, often found in trusses and frames.

q: 135. A simply supported beam is subjected to a central concentrated load. The slope at the two ends is given by
explain: For a simply supported beam with a central load W, the maximum slope (θ) at the supports is WL² / 16EI.

q: 136. A simply supported beam of span L carries a uniformly distributed load W. The maximum bending moment M is
explain: For a SS beam with total UDL 'W' (where W = w * L), the maximum bending moment at the center is WL/8 (or wL²/8).

q: 137. A simply supported beam of span L carries a concentrated load W at its mid-span. The maximum bending moment M is
explain: The maximum bending moment for a central point load on a simply supported beam occurs at the center and is equal to WL/4.

q: 138. A simply supported beam carries two equal concentrated loads W at distances L/3 from either support. The max BM is
explain: The reactions are W at each support. The BM between the two loads is constant and equal to Reaction * Distance = W * (L/3) = WL/3.

q: 139. The maximum deflection of a simply supported beam of length L with a central load W, is
explain: Standard deflection formula for a SS beam with central point load: δ = WL³ / 48EI.

q: 140. The ratio of max deflections of a SS beam with an isolated central load and that of with a UDL over its entire length, is
explain: Deflection(Point) = WL³/48EI. Deflection(UDL) = 5WL³/384EI. The ratio is (1/48) / (5/384) = 8/5 = 24/15.

q: 141. The ratio of max deflection of a cantilever beam with an isolated load at free end and with a UDL over its entire length, is
explain: Deflection(Point) = WL³/3EI. Deflection(UDL) = WL³/8EI. The ratio is (1/3) / (1/8) = 8/3.

q: 142. Maximum deflection of a cantilever due to pure bending moment M at its free end, is
explain: Using the moment-area method, the deflection at the free end for a constant moment M is ML² / 2EI.

q: 143. A cantilever beam... load at free end. If the width of the beam is doubled, the deflection... will be changed in the ratio of
explain: Deflection is inversely proportional to Moment of Inertia (I). For a rectangle, I = bd³/12. If width 'b' is doubled, I doubles, and deflection becomes 1/2.

q: 144. If the length of a cantilever carrying an isolated load at its free end is doubled, the deflection... will increase by
explain: Deflection is proportional to L³. If length L is doubled, deflection increases by 2³ = 8 times.

q: 145. If the width of a simply supported beam carrying an isolated load at its centre is doubled, the deflection... is changed by
explain: Since deflection is inversely proportional to I (and thus width b), doubling the width reduces the deflection to half (1/2).

q: 146. If the depth of a simply supported beam carrying an isolated load at its centre, is doubled, the deflection... will be changed by a factor of
explain: Deflection is inversely proportional to I, which is proportional to d³. Doubling depth d makes deflection 1 / (2³) = 1/8.

q: 147. If the width b and depth d of a beam simply supported with a central load are interchanged, the deflection... will be changed in the ratio of
explain: Deflection 1 ∝ 1/(bd³). Deflection 2 ∝ 1/(db³). Ratio Δ2/Δ1 = (bd³) / (db³) = d²/b² = (d/b)².

q: 148. The deflection of any rectangular beam simply supported, is
options: inversely proportional to the cube of its depth
directly proportional to the cube of its length
explain: Based on the formula δ = WL³ / 48EI and I = bd³/12, deflection is inversely proportional to the width (b) and the cube of the depth (d³).

q: 149. A rectangular beam of length l supported at its two ends carries a central point load W. The maximum deflection occurs
explain: For a symmetrical loading on a simply supported beam, the maximum deflection always occurs at the mid-span (center).

q: 150. The maximum deflection of a cantilever beam of length l with a point load W at the free end is
explain: The standard formula for maximum deflection at the free end of a cantilever with a point load is Wl³ / 3EI.

q: 151. The maximum deflection of a fixed beam carrying a central point load lies at
explain: Due to symmetry in both loading and support conditions, the maximum deflection of a fixed beam with a central point load occurs at the mid-span.

q: 152. The maximum deflection of a fixed beam of length l carrying a central point load W is
explain: The deflection of a fixed beam is 1/4th of the deflection of a simply supported beam of the same span and load. Since SS beam deflection is Wl³/48EI, fixed beam deflection is Wl³/192EI.

q: 153. The product of Young's modulus (E) and moment of inertia (I) is known as
explain: Flexural rigidity (EI) represents the resistance offered by a beam section against bending deformation.

q: 154. The expression EI (d⁴y/dx⁴) at any section for a beam is equal to
explain: In the differential equation of beams, the fourth derivative of deflection multiplied by EI represents the rate of loading (w).

q: 155. A beam which is fixed at one end and free at the other is called
explain: A cantilever is a rigid structural element that extends horizontally and is supported at only one end.

q: 156. A beam extending beyond the support is called
explain: An overhanging beam has one or both of its end portions extending beyond the supports.

q: 157. A beam encastered at both the ends is called
explain: A fixed beam (also known as a built-in or encastered beam) has both ends restrained against rotation and displacement.

q: 158. A beam supported on more than two supports is called
explain: A continuous beam is a statically indeterminate structure that spans across more than two supports.

q: 159. A cantilever beam is one which is
options: fixed at one end and free at the other end
supported on more than two supports
explain: The defining characteristic of a cantilever is the single fixed support that provides all the necessary stability.

q: 160. A continuous beam is one which is
options: fixed at one end and free at the other end
supported on more than two supports
explain: Any beam having three or more supports is classified as a continuous beam.

q: 161. A concentrated load is one which
options: acts at a point on a beam
spreads non-uniformly over the whole length
spreads uniformly over the whole length
varies uniformly over the whole length
explain: A concentrated or point load is assumed to act at a single specific point on the beam's axis.

q: 162. The bending moment on a section is maximum where shear force is
explain: Since dM/dx = V, the maximum bending moment occurs where the shear force (V) is zero or changes sign.

q: 163. When a load on the free end of a cantilever beam is increased, failure will occur
options: in the middle of the beam
at a distance 2l/3 from free end
explain: In a cantilever, both the Shear Force and Bending Moment are maximum at the fixed support, making it the most critical section for failure.

q: 164. The bending moment at the free end of a cantilever beam is
explain: Since there are no forces or moments acting beyond the free end, the internal bending moment at that point must be zero.

q: 165. The shear force of a cantilever beam of length l carrying a uniformly distributed load of w per unit length is... at the fixed end.
explain: The total load on the beam is w * l. To maintain equilibrium, the vertical reaction (Shear Force) at the fixed end must equal the total load.

q: 166. The shear force diagram of a cantilever beam of length l and carrying a uniformly distributed load of w per unit length will be
explain: The SF varies linearly from zero at the free end to wl at the fixed end, forming a right-angled triangle.

q: 167. The bending moment of a cantilever beam of length l and carrying a uniformly distributed load of w per unit length is... at the free end.
explain: As per the definition of Bending Moment, the sum of moments of forces to the right of the free end is zero.

q: 168. The shear force and bending moment are zero at the free end of a cantilever beam, if it carries a
options: point load at the free end
point load at the middle of its length
uniformly distributed load over the whole length
explain: If a load is at the middle, the section from the middle to the free end has no load acting on it, resulting in zero SF and BM in that portion.

q: 169. The bending moment of a cantilever beam of length l and carrying a uniformly distributed load of w per unit length is... at the fixed end.
explain: The total load is 'wl' acting at its center of gravity (l/2 from the support). Moment = (wl) * (l/2) = wl²/2.

q: 170. The shear force of a cantilever beam... carrying a gradually varying load from zero at the free end and w per unit length at the fixed end is... at the fixed end.
explain: The total load is the area of the triangular loading diagram: 1/2 * base * height = 1/2 * l * w = wl/2.

q: 171. The bending moment of a cantilever beam... carrying a gradually varying load from zero at free end and w per unit length at the fixed end is... at the fixed end.
explain: Total load wl/2 acts at a distance of l/3 from the base (fixed end). Moment = (wl/2) * (l/3) = wl²/6.

q: 172. The maximum bending moment of a simply supported beam of span l and carrying a point load w at the centre of beam, is
explain: Reaction at each support is w/2. Maximum BM at the center = (w/2) * (l/2) = wl/4.

q: 173. The bending moment diagram for a simply supported beam loaded in its centre is
explain: The BM increases linearly from zero at both supports to wl/4 at the center, forming an isosceles triangle.

q: 174. The shear force in the centre of a simply supported beam carrying a uniformly distributed load of w per unit length, is
explain: For a symmetrical UDL on an SS beam, the SF diagram passes through zero at the mid-span.

q: 175. The bending moment in the centre of a simply supported beam carrying a uniformly distributed load of w per unit length is
explain: The reaction is wl/2. BM at center = (wl/2 * l/2) - (w * l/2 * l/4) = wl²/4 - wl²/8 = wl²/8.

q: 176. The shear force at the ends of a simply supported beam carrying a uniformly distributed load of w per unit length is
options: wl at one end and -wl at the other end
wl/2 at one end and -wl/2 at the other end
wl²/2 at one end and -wl²/2 at the other end
explain: For a symmetrical UDL, each support reaction is half the total load (W = wl). Therefore, the shear force starts at +wl/2 at one support and ends at -wl/2 at the other.

q: 177. The shear force diagram for a simply supported beam carrying a uniformly distributed load of w per unit length, consists of
explain: The SFD for a UDL on an SS beam is a straight line passing through zero at the center, creating two equal right-angled triangles on either side of the mid-span.

q: 178. The bending moment diagram for a simply supported beam carrying a uniformly distributed load of w per unit length, will be
explain: Since the shear force varies linearly (1st degree) for a UDL, the bending moment (which is the integral of SF) varies parabolically (2nd degree).

q: 179. The shear force at the centre of a simply supported beam with a gradually varying load from zero at both ends to w per metre at the centre, is
explain: Due to the symmetry of the triangular loading (zero at ends, max at center), the shear force at the exact mid-point of the span must be zero.

q: 180. The point of contra flexure is a point where
explain: The point of contraflexure (or inflection) is the location in a structural member where the bending moment changes from positive (sagging) to negative (hogging) or vice versa.

q: 181. When shear force at a point is zero, then bending moment is... at that point.
explain: Mathematically, V = dM/dx. If the derivative (V) is zero, the function (M) is at a local maximum or minimum.

q: 182. In a simply supported beam carrying uniformly distributed load w per unit length, the point of contraflexure
options: lies in the centre of the beam
lies at the ends of the beam
depends upon the length of beam
explain: In a simply supported beam with downward UDL, the entire beam experiences sagging (positive BM). Since the sign never changes, there is no point of contraflexure.

q: 183. When there is a sudden increase or decrease in shear force diagram between any two points, it indicates that there is a
options: point load at the two points
no loading between the two points
uniformly distributed load between the two points
uniformly varying load between the two points
explain: A vertical jump in the shear force diagram always corresponds to the application of a concentrated (point) load at 그 point.

q: 184. When the shear force diagram is a parabolic curve between two points, it indicates that there is a
options: point load at the two points
no loading between the two points
uniformly distributed load between the two points
uniformly varying load between the two points
explain: If the loading is linear (uniformly varying), the shear force (its integral) will be a 2nd-degree parabolic curve.

q: 185. In a beam where shear force changes sign, the bending moment will be
explain: A change in sign in the SFD indicates that the SF passes through zero, which identifies the location of the maximum bending moment.

q: 186. The point of contraflexure occurs in
explain: Overhanging beams typically experience hogging over the supports and sagging in the span, creating points where the bending moment must pass through zero.

q: 187. The number of reaction components possible at a hinge on rollers supports is
explain: A roller support only resists movement perpendicular to the surface it sits on, providing exactly one vertical reaction component.

q: 188. The number of reaction components possible at a hinged end for a general loading is
explain: A hinged (pinned) support prevents horizontal and vertical displacement but allows rotation, resulting in two reaction components (Rx and Ry).

q: 189. The number of reaction components possible at a fixed or built in end for a general loading
explain: A fixed support prevents all movement (vertical, horizontal, and rotation), providing three reactions: vertical force, horizontal force, and a bending moment.

q: 190. A simply supported beam is subjected to a pure moment. This will be resisted through
options: a moment reaction at hinged end
a moment reaction at hinge on rollers end
a couple formed by the reaction from the two supports
external support capable of resisting moment
explain: Since simple supports cannot provide moment reactions, the applied moment is balanced by a couple consisting of two equal and opposite vertical reactions at the supports.

q: 191. A cantilever beam is the one which is supported with
options: one end hinge and other on rollers
one end fixed and the other on rollers
one end fixed and the other free
explain: A cantilever is defined by having one end entirely fixed (built-in) and the other end completely unsupported (free).

q: 192. A horizontal beam with both the ends hinged will be statically determinate for this type of loadings
explain: If both ends are hinged, there are 4 unknown reactions. For purely vertical loads, horizontal reactions are zero, reducing unknowns and making it determinate with basic equilibrium equations.

q: 193. A beam is said to be in general, stable and statically determinate for general loading when the number of reaction components is
explain: In 2D space, there are 3 equations of equilibrium (ΣFx, ΣFy, ΣM). A structure with 3 independent reaction components is statically determinate.

q: 194. The shear force on a simply supported beam is proportional to
options: algebraic sum of the transverse forces of the section
explain: By definition, the shear force at any section of a beam is the algebraic sum of all external transverse forces acting on either side of that section.

q: 195. A cantilever beam carrying a uniformly distributed load W over its full length is propped at its free end... BM will be zero at its free end also at
explain: For a propped cantilever with UDL, the point of zero bending moment (contraflexure) occurs at a distance of 3/4L from the fixed end (or 1/4L from the prop).

q: 196. A simply supported beam carrying a UDL... is propped at the centre... The reaction of the prop will be
explain: By equating the downward deflection of a SS beam due to UDL (5wL⁴/384EI) to the upward deflection due to the prop (PL³/48EI), the prop reaction is found to be 5/8 of the total load W.

q: 197. A uniform girder simply supported at its ends... propped at the centre so as to neutralize the deflection. The net B.M. at the centre will be
explain: With a prop reaction of 5/8W, the net BM at the center becomes (WL/8) - (5/8W * L/4) = WL/32.

q: 198. The moment diagram for a cantilever whose free end is subjected to a bending moment, will be a
explain: If a constant moment is applied at the end, the internal bending moment is uniform throughout the length, resulting in a rectangular BMD.

q: 199. The moment diagram for a cantilever carrying linearly varying load from zero at its free end and to maximum at the fixed end will be
explain: Since the load is linear (1st degree), the shear force is parabolic (2nd degree) and the bending moment is a cubic parabola (3rd degree).

q: 200. The moment diagram for a cantilever which is subjected to a uniformly distributed load will be a
explain: For a UDL (0th degree), the shear force is linear (1st degree) and the bending moment is parabolic (2nd degree).
